title: Performance
summary:
This part settles how fast, small and lean RichView must be after the rewrite, how that is measured, which numbers run in the fast gate, the release run per `pre-prod` batch and the full capture before a `prod` merge (DEL-81). It covers every budget in `docs/PERFORMANCE.md`, the measurements that never had one (MCP tools, CLI checks, the chart kernel, PDF export, report and site weight, first paint, layout shift, hydration, frame pacing, interaction and preview latency, editor, MCP, server and browser memory, install size, build and test time) and targets beyond today. Which checks run in which test tier is part 02's; PRF-51 only sets durations.

State on 2026-10-21: on Claw Mini, `b4db233` passes 24 of 25 budgets; the 25th, a Linux-only memory gate, cannot run on macOS. The last recorded capture (Linux, 2026-10-12) failed 6 of 25, and no budget has ever blocked a merge: PR #22 merged with the Wasm over its limit. Costs drift inside the headroom: the Wasm uses 96.6 % of its budget since the font catalog moved out of it; the small report's HTML without the runtime doubled since 2026-10-04, mostly because its style, scientific, now embeds six faces instead of three; the dense editor and the MCP server each hold about 1.5 GiB after a session; and on the phone profile the small report's first chart turns live after 8.2 s.

The decisions that matter most: Claw Mini as the reference host, with a lock and an outside-CPU check instead of waiting for a quiet machine (PRF-01, PRF-02); no timing budget in the fast gate, a short performance set in each release run and the full capture, phone profile and WebKit included, daily on a changed `pre-prod` head and before each `prod` merge (PRF-04); a ratchet from the legacy baseline whose regressions merge only on the feature or design card that needs them (PRF-05, PRF-08); a report runtime of at most 512 KiB embedded in every report (PRF-31); and memory budgets on physical footprint for native processes and on renderer memory for browser pages (PRF-03, PRF-40 to PRF-44).

Answer together with other parts: PRF-02, PRF-04 and PRF-24 with DEL-08, DEL-33, DEL-51 and DEL-62; PRF-05 and PRF-08 with DEL-34 and DEL-36; PRF-31 with INT-04, ARC-06, ARC-24 and FEA-RP-38; PRF-07, PRF-20 and PRF-33 with the removal of `/charts/` (ARC-40, FEA-SF-44); PRF-14 with FEA-SF-17; PRF-17 with ARC-48 and ARC-49; PRF-18 with INT-35.

Captures cited in the cards: **10-04 Linux** is the integration capture `faff365` on an Intel i7-12700H, Linux, powersave governor, load 0.9 at start and 9.7 at the end; values quoted from `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` at `2c926b0` come from the first capture on the same host that day and say so. **10-12 Linux** is `9b300f0` on the same CPU as a shared host with four pinned cores, not quiet. **10-21 M4** is `b4db233` on Claw Mini (Apple M4, 10 cores, 16 GiB, macOS 26.3): the harness ran at load 3.7–4.7 and the whole checks session at 2.6–7.3. Lockdown probes ran on 2026-10-21 at load 2.0–4.7 and on 2026-10-22 at 1.8–3.1. Hosts and some fixtures differ, so read the columns as ranges, not a trend. Compact copies of the 2026-10-21 capture and of every probe, with their methods, are in `docs/lockdown/evidence/performance/`.

How to answer: accept keeps the proposal as written; edit rewrites it (a number, a scope or a method); reject drops it from the rewrite; defer leaves it open. Budgets for surfaces whose survival parts 03 and 04 decide (editor service, render API, published-report serving, Publish, PDF export, Node packages, the landing demo) apply only if the surface stays. Items marked informational never block a merge. Part 08's cross-part contradiction cards (OPN-50 to OPN-68) decide conflicts involving this part's cards and should be answered first.

items.title: Reference host for every budget
items.question: Which machine's measurements decide whether a performance budget passes?
items.why: `docs/PERFORMANCE.md` names no machine, so the same budgets pass or fail by host: every endpoint that failed on the shared Linux host on 2026-10-12 ran 2.8–4.6× faster on the M4 on 2026-10-21 and passed. A budget can only gate merges if one host owns it. Part 02 already runs the gate only on Claw Mini (DEL-22). The answer also decides where test-tier durations (PRF-51) are judged.
items.proposed: Claw Mini (Mac mini, Apple M4, 10 cores, 16 GiB, macOS) is the reference host. Every budget in this part is defined, measured and gated there, under PRF-02's lock and outside-CPU check, with the Rust toolchain and Playwright browsers pinned by the repository. A capture from any other machine is a disclosure that names its host and is never compared with reference numbers. Replacing the host, its macOS major version, the toolchain or the Playwright version re-captures every budget and starts a new baseline, reported in the next review packet.

items.title: Timing captures on a busy host
items.question: When does a timing capture count, and what happens when the host is busy?
items.why: Claw Mini runs several agents and system services at once. The 2026-10-21 harness started at load 4.66, the whole session ran at 2.6–7.3 and the probes at 2.0–4.7; a two-minute sample on 2026-10-22 showed load 1.8–2.6 with 0.5–1.4 cores busy, the largest share from a macOS file-provider daemon that no RichView lock controls. The harness itself raises load (0.9 to 9.7 during the 2026-10-04 capture), so a load threshold cannot separate foreign work from the benchmark, and none of the cited captures would have met a start threshold of 2.0. Instruction counts of repeated CLI renders vary by at most 1.5 % once the first run is discarded, while wall-time p95 sits 4–14 % above the median within one capture (PRF-05). The development-harness brief asked for 'resource-aware build coordination'.
items.proposed: A timing capture holds the RichView build coordinator's exclusive lock while it measures, so no RichView agent build, test or browser starts during that window; other projects' agents and system services are outside the lock. Under DEL-81 captures run once per release batch into `pre-prod` and in the full run before a candidate, not on every merge into `dev`, so development agents wait only for those windows; the release run builds in its own target folder, so its build never holds the streams' lock. During the capture, CPU used outside the harness's process tree is sampled every second; if it averages more than one core, or any sample exceeds four, the capture is inconclusive and repeats once, and a second inconclusive capture holds the merge as 'performance inconclusive'. In the release run, native costs are judged by instruction counts and browser timings against the base build measured interleaved in the same capture (PRF-05), so a busy host slows a capture without changing its verdict; absolute millisecond limits are judged on the full capture (PRF-04). A day of logged host activity confirms or resets the one-core and four-core thresholds before the gate is switched on. Size, memory and instruction-count checks run regardless of load, and every capture records load and outside CPU before, during and after.

options.label: Lock, outside-CPU check and interleaved base runs
options.detail: Verdicts do not depend on other agents; a capture repeats when the host is very busy, and the lock binds only RichView agents.

options.label: Wait for a load average of 2.0 first

options.label: Run anyway and record load
options.detail: Never waits; verdicts depend on other agents, as on 2026-10-12 (6 of 25 failed).

items.recommendation: Lock, outside-CPU check and interleaved base runs: the host is never quiet, so release verdicts must not depend on it.

items.title: Memory and timing measures on macOS
items.question: How does RichView measure memory and timing on the reference host, and what is left for Linux captures?
items.why: The only memory gate parses Linux `VmHWM`, so on the reference host it fails closed by design. macOS reports a process's physical footprint, which counts the memory the process holds, including what its allocator keeps after freeing: `/usr/bin/time -l` prints the peak for a process that exits, and `footprint` and `vmmap` sample a live one. Allocators differ: the dense editor peaked at 98.6 MiB `VmHWM` on Linux (2026-10-04, `2c926b0`) but held a 1,538 MiB footprint after 100 previews on macOS (2026-10-22), almost all of it freed blocks the allocator keeps (PRF-41). For browser pages, Chromium reports its process IDs over the DevTools protocol and `ps` reads their resident memory.
items.proposed: Native processes are budgeted on peak physical footprint as macOS reports it on the reference host: at exit for processes that end (CLI, PDF export), and sampled through the session for long-lived ones (editor service, MCP server, server). Browser pages are budgeted on the resident memory of their renderer process. Timing runs discard the first launch of every newly built binary, which costs 0.2–0.6 s on macOS. Linux peak-memory captures may be kept as disclosures, separate and never compared with macOS numbers; the Linux-only memory gate is retired.

options.detail: Gates run on the reference host; stricter than Linux where the macOS allocator keeps freed memory.

options.label: Gate on both
options.detail: Two hosts and two baselines for every release run.

items.title: Which budgets run in the fast gate, the release run and the full run
items.question: Which performance checks run in the fast gate, which in the release run that takes a batch of `dev` merges into `pre-prod`, and which only in the full run before a prod merge?
items.why: Development agents merge into `dev` after the fast gate alone (unit tests, ideally under five seconds), and the release agent runs the long suites on each batch of up to 20 merges before `pre-prod` takes it (Daniel's DEL-81 answer). Daniel reviews only design and feature decisions. Today no budget blocks anything: CI never runs the checker, the 2026-10-12 capture failed 6 of 25 without consequence, and PR #22 merged with the Wasm at 1,601,334 B against a 1,572,864 B limit. Today's harness took 157.2 s on 2026-10-21 for 25 endpoints, one engine and the desktop only. This part adds repeats (PRF-06), interleaved base runs (PRF-05), the phone profile, WebKit, PDF, memory sessions, build and tier timings and new endpoints: about 15–20 minutes in all, by this part's estimate. DEL-08's former per-merge gate took about 12.5–15 minutes with today's harness; DEL-81 replaces it with the fast gate and the release run.
items.proposed:
| Set | Runs on | Budgets | Estimated capture |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fast gate | every push to `dev` (`rv-gate fast`, DEL-81) | none: unit tests of what the change can affect; an agent may run a budget check by hand when it judges that useful | none |
| Release run | each batch merged from `dev` into `pre-prod` (`rv-gate release`, DEL-81), for what the batch affects | sizes (PRF-30 to PRF-32, PRF-39); instruction counts and footprints of CLI renders and the chart kernel (PRF-05, PRF-19, PRF-40); native, CLI and MCP latency (PRF-10 to PRF-13); Chromium desktop timings against interleaved base runs (PRF-20 to PRF-23, PRF-25, PRF-29, PRF-33, PRF-38) | about 4 minutes |
| Full | on `pre-prod` before a candidate and on each prod candidate (`rv-gate full` and `rv-gate prod`, DEL-33), and once a day on a changed `pre-prod` head | everything above, plus the phone profile (PRF-26, PRF-34 to PRF-36), WebKit (PRF-24, PRF-27), PDF (PRF-16), memory sessions (PRF-41 to PRF-44), server and published reads (PRF-14, PRF-15), build and tier durations (PRF-50, PRF-51), and every absolute millisecond limit | about 15–20 minutes |

A release-run failure fails the batch: the release agent bisects it to the merge that caused it and fixes forward on `dev` or reverts that merge (DEL-81). A full-run failure is bisected the same way, before the review packet is built (DEL-34); `prod` is cut only from a `pre-prod` head with a passing full receipt for the exact candidate (DEL-04, DEL-71). Informational items (PRF-60 to PRF-62) are reported and never block. No budget is waived for a single batch; changing a limit is an edit to this lockdown, held for Daniel under DEL-36.

items.title: Regression gate against an accepted baseline
items.question: Besides absolute limits, how much may a single merge make RichView slower, bigger or hungrier, and who accepts a regression?
items.why: Absolute timing limits leave 1.8–15× headroom on the M4 and the Wasm limit 3.4 %, so a merge can double a cost and still pass, and growth adds up: the small report's HTML without the runtime doubled between 2026-10-04 and 2026-10-21 (117,450 to 233,789 B), mainly because the scientific style the fixtures use went from 3 to 6 embedded faces (beb330f), while the flagship grew 1.7× and the dense fixture 1.1× on fixtures that also changed. The CPU instruction count of a CLI render is stable once the first run of a new binary is discarded: 0.1–0.4 % across 7 runs on 2026-10-22, and at most 1.5 % in earlier 3- and 5-run series, whose first runs differed by +15 % (small) and −7 % (flagship). The 2026-10-04 chart-kernel regressions of 24.7–28.1 % were disclosed and never gated.
items.proposed: Each release run compares the batch's combined `pre-prod` state with the accepted baseline, a stored receipt that changes only as described here; PRF-08 names the first one. The release run fails, and the release agent bisects it to the merge that caused the regression (DEL-81), when the Wasm or any fixture's HTML grows by more than 16 KiB, a shipped binary by more than 64 KiB after gzip, the CPU instructions a CLI render or the chart-kernel benchmark executes (median of 7 runs after one discarded run) by more than 5 %, or peak footprint by more than 10 %, or when a browser endpoint's p95 is more than 20 % slower than the base build measured interleaved in the same capture. An improvement beyond these margins lowers the baseline automatically. A regression beyond them stays only when the merge that caused it is a declared feature or design PR (DEL-32) whose card states the cost; otherwise the release agent fixes it forward or reverts that merge (DEL-81). Daniel's answer to the feature or design card accepts the cost and raises the baseline, which is the hold DEL-36 requires for a raised baseline. Fixes and refactors (`decision: none`) never raise it.

options.label: Ratchet, cost on the feature or design card
options.detail: Stops creep; Daniel sees a cost only with the feature or design that needs it, and fixes can never add one.

options.label: Ratchet, agents accept up to the absolute limits
options.detail: Fewer cards; each accepted regression goes with its reason to the DEL-34 appendix, and DEL-36 must exempt performance baselines.

options.label: Compare with the previous `pre-prod` head
options.detail: Simpler; allows unlimited creep in steps below the margins.

options.label: Absolute limits only
options.detail: Today's rule; regressions hide inside the headroom.

items.recommendation: Ratchet, cost on the feature or design card: regressions stay visible, and Daniel decides them only where he already decides the feature.

items.title: Evidence integrity, sample sizes and harnesses
items.question: What makes a performance capture valid evidence, and which harnesses stay?
items.why: The checker's seven integrity checks flagged the 2026-10-12 capture (6 of 7 passed). The browser harness keeps its own copy of eight limits and throws when one fails, so a slow run surfaces as an integrity failure in addition to the budget verdicts, and the limits are defined twice. Dense edit and cold mount each rest on a single event. Some harnesses only compare with implementations the rewrite retires: `scripts/benchmark-baseline.mjs` with the TypeScript renderer and `scripts/benchmark-preview.py` with the archived Rust preview; the Node boundary harness takes 49 s per capture and gates nothing.
items.proposed: A capture is valid only when it records the commit, artifact and fixture hashes, host, OS, toolchain and browser versions, load and outside CPU before, during and after (PRF-02), and sample counts, and the seven integrity checks pass. Limits live in one file; harnesses measure and never judge. Every p95 uses at least 20 samples, and at least 100 when the value is under 10 ms. Single-event endpoints (large-source edit, cold mount, first paint, PDF export) repeat at least 5 times: the median must meet the limit and no repeat may exceed 1.5× it. Missing evidence fails. Every harness feeds a budget in this part or is deleted: the boundary harness goes with the Node packages (PRF-17), the TypeScript and archived-preview comparisons are deleted, and the chart-kernel benchmark feeds PRF-19. Each capture's compact outputs are kept with its gate receipt (DEL-20).

items.title: First baseline and the rewrite period
items.question: Which capture starts the regression ratchet, and how do budgets apply while the rewrite replaces legacy code on `dev`?
items.why: `dev` starts from `main` as DEL-02 renames it `prod`, which part 08 first makes equal to richview.ai: `b4db233` plus PR #69 (OPN-01; FEA-SF-30 rules out any hotfix), and which since 2026-10-26 also holds PR #70 (97ac0d0, INT-52). INT-70 measures the rewrite against `b4db233`. PRF-05 needs a first accepted baseline, and during the rewrite most merges replace a legacy component or rebuild a feature, so most change a measured cost. That legacy tree already fails several budgets proposed here (editor and MCP memory, phone long frames, landing weight, WebKit pacing). Endpoints of dropped surfaces (`/charts/`, the render API, the Node packages) lose their baseline, and new ones (docs gallery, landing first visit, MCP memory) have none.
items.proposed: The first accepted baseline is the full capture of the commit `dev` starts from (D-PROD-BASELINE). From the first release run (DEL-81), PRF-05's ratchet compares each release batch with it. A budget that baseline already fails is listed as a known failure in every review packet: a merge may not make it worse, and once a capture meets it, it gates like any other. Rewriting a component is a feature PR under DEL-32, so a cost it adds rides on its feature card (PRF-05). An endpoint whose surface is dropped leaves the baseline with the merge that drops it; a new endpoint enters with its first full capture, and until then only its absolute limits apply. Each review packet also reports the INT-70 comparison with `b4db233` for every endpoint both trees have.

options.label: Legacy capture as the first baseline
options.detail: The rewrite cannot end bigger or slower than today without a card that says why; known failures can only improve.

options.label: First complete rewrite capture as the baseline
options.detail: Absolute limits only until the rewritten product has every endpoint; regressions against legacy show only in INT-70's report.

ARC-39 keeps the landing page and ARC-38 the playground, but no budget covers either. Lockdown probes on the M4 (Chromium 153, loopback with gzip, 2026-10-21 landing, 2026-10-22 playground):

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bytes transferred | 3,793,608 | 3,793,608 | 1,858,444 | 1,858,444 |
| First contentful paint | 48–152 ms | 708–712 ms | 25–143 ms | 244–248 ms |

items.proposed: On a first visit, median of 5 loads with no load over 1.5× the limit: the landing page's largest contentful paint is ≤ 1.5 s on the phone profile and ≤ 200 ms on the desktop profile, its layout shift is ≤ 0.01, and it transfers ≤ 1 MB before the reader scrolls or types; the playground's first live preview chart appears in ≤ 500 ms on the desktop profile. On the phone profile the playground is reported, not gated, because the site runtime alone takes about 9 s at Slow 4G (PRF-30).

items.title: Site caching, compression and bytes per view
items.question: How do richview.ai and the report host serve their runtime and font files, and how are bytes per view tracked?
items.why: On 2026-10-22 live richview.ai (PR #69 build) served its HTML and runtime files with `cache-control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` under fixed names such as `richview_web_bg.wasm`, so every visit revalidates each file before using it. It does serve Brotli: the Wasm arrives as 1,403,188 B against 4,368,091 B raw and the font catalog as 322,214 B. Loopback probes measured 3.79 MB for a first landing visit, 1.86 MB for the playground and 1.76–3.00 MB for the small and flagship reports. INT-15 asks for low, explainable operating cost with a written estimate for each hosted feature. `docs/PERFORMANCE.md:21` says loopback results are not production guarantees, and nothing measures the live host after a deploy; DEL-40 checks the live routes against the gate's captures.
items.proposed: Site files other than HTML get content-hashed names and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`; HTML pages revalidate on every visit. Text, JavaScript, CSS and Wasm are served Brotli-compressed. The report host serves its report runtime and font routes the same way (ARC-24): content-hashed URLs with that immutable `Cache-Control`, the runtime Brotli-compressed and the WOFF2 fonts as stored, each kept while a stored report links it (ARC-21). A story's pages and each version's link-preview thumbnail (ARC-69) are not site files: they sit behind the story's access check (TYP-70), at routes named by slug and version, never by content hash. A story shared with anyone on the web sends `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` on the versioned routes and `no-cache` on the latest routes; a story shared only with signed-in readers sends `private, no-store` on every one of them, and every response varies on the session, so no shared cache can keep a private story or answer a later request after the story is unshared; report pages follow TYP-70. After each deploy (DEL-40), a check fetches the live landing, playground and docs pages and records bytes, encodings and cache headers against the gate's capture; a mismatch is a defect. Each review packet reports bytes per first and repeat visit for those pages, the report fixtures and the hosted small fixture (PRF-32), the basis of INT-15's cost estimate.

options.label: Hashed names, immutable caching
options.detail: Repeat visits move no runtime bytes and make no revalidation round trips; every build renames the changed files, which the build manifest records (ARC-46).

options.label: Revalidate every visit
options.detail: Today's headers; a repeat visit waits for a round trip per file before it can use its cached copy.

items.recommendation: Hashed names, immutable caching.
